platforms.title: Adult Fever: When Should You Actually See a Doctor?
platforms.meta_description: NHS advice on adult fever: what counts as a high temperature, how to measure it, safe paracetamol limits, hidden paracetamol in flu remedies, when to call 111.
platforms.body_html:
You wake up shivery, your back feels hot, and the thermometer in the bathroom drawer says 38.4. For most adults the next questions are practical: is this a GP problem, and how much paracetamol can you actually take? The NHS answer to the first part is reassuring. A high temperature is usually your body fighting an infection such as a cold or flu, and it is not usually a sign of anything serious. The useful skill is knowing which details change that picture.

Adult Fever: When Should You Actually See a Doctor?

According to the NHS page on high temperature in adults, a fever is usually considered to be 38C or above. Normal body temperature differs from person to person and shifts during the day, so the number is a guide rather than a verdict. The NHS also points out that you may have a high temperature even if the thermometer reads below 38C when you feel hot, cold or shivery. You do not have to own a thermometer at all; a chest or back that feels hotter than usual counts as a sign too.

If you do measure, method matters. The NHS recommends a digital thermometer placed under the tongue towards the back of the mouth, with lips closed until it beeps, or held tight in the armpit. A digital ear thermometer is fine if you follow its instructions. What it advises against is just as useful: do not rely on forehead strips, because they are not accurate, and avoid glass thermometers, which can be dangerous. One reliable reading beats five readings from a strip.

Why does a fever make you feel so rough? The temperature itself is part of the immune response, but it comes with sweating, chills and fluid loss. That is why the NHS treatment advice starts with fluids rather than tablets: drink enough water that your pee is light yellow and clear, get plenty of rest, and try to stay at home away from other people until the high temperature has gone.

4 Rules for Taking Paracetamol Safely With a Fever

The NHS says you can take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel uncomfortable, which is a different goal from forcing the number down. The NHS paracetamol guidance for adults spells out the label limits. First, for standard 500mg tablets one dose is 1 or 2 tablets, with at least 4 hours between doses. Second, never take more than 8 tablets in 24 hours. If you weigh less than 50kg you may need a lower dose, so check the packet or ask a pharmacist.

Third, count every product, not just the box labelled paracetamol. The NHS warns against taking paracetamol at the same time as other medicines containing it, such as cold and flu remedies, because you may take too much, which can be dangerous. A hot lemon sachet plus two tablets can quietly exceed the limit. If you have taken more than the packet says, get help from NHS 111, and if you are sent to A&E, do not drive yourself.

Fourth, set a time limit. NHS guidance says do not take paracetamol for more than 3 days unless a doctor tells you to. It may not be suitable if you have a kidney or liver condition or are dependent on alcohol. Adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, but the NHS suggests trying each on its own first and using the lowest dose that works.

You Don't Have to Bring Every Fever Down

A temperature that sits at 38C while you rest on the sofa is doing a job. The NHS urgent advice is about the trend, not a single reading: ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you have been treating it at home and it is not getting better or is getting worse. A very high temperature, or one that will not come down, can occasionally point to something more serious, which is exactly when a clinician should take over.

If you remember one thing, make it this: paracetamol is for comfort, capped at 8 standard tablets a day and 3 days without medical advice, and a fever that keeps climbing despite rest and fluids is a reason to call 111 rather than to add another remedy. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a doctor or pharmacist.

Sources: NHS, "High temperature (fever) in adults" (reviewed May 2023); NHS, "Paracetamol for adults: how and when to take or use paracetamol" and "Who can and cannot take paracetamol".
